stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 7.1 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 314 K and 1.02 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 37.0 mL of 0.17 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.11 M NaOH.
5.4 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 59 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 8.2 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Na (Z = 11) and Mg (Z = 12) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of $$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.01 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 27 g. The actual yield is 21.1 g. What is the percent yield?
145 g of water at 77 °C is mixed with 52 g of water at 21 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 24 min. Starting at 19 M, what is the concentration after 72 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

options.text: Their ions move freely in the solid
options.why: Ions are fixed in the lattice.

options.text: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 13. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: If ΔH = −286 kJ for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), what is ΔH for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂ + O₂?
Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, CO2 44, H2 2.02, Cl2 70.9.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 37. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgO}$$ or $$\ce{LiF}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{MgO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{LiF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{LiF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic

questions.explanation: MgO has ion charges 2 and 2; LiF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.19 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.409 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 93 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Which element has the highest electronegativity?

options.why: Correct. Electronegativity increases up and to the right.

questions.explanation: Electronegativity increases up and to the right.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of S in $$\ce{SO4^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CH4 16, CO2 44, O2 32, Ar 40.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 38 L flask at 1.58 atm and 331 K?
A reaction has ΔG° = −50 kJ/mol but does not occur noticeably at room temperature. The best explanation is:

options.why: Negative ΔG° means K greater than 1.

options.text: It has a high activation energy, so it is under kinetic control
options.why: Correct. Favorable is not the same as fast.

questions.explanation: Favorable is not the same as fast.

questions.stem: What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{CO2}$$?

options.why: Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 36 L flask at 0.443 atm and 256 K?
For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 1.4. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.4 M and [C] = 0.7 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.45
options.why: If Q is greater than K, the reaction proceeds in reverse.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 2.45
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 2.45, which is greater than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 3.5

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of iron (Fe, Z = 26)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 26 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography with a nonpolar solvent, which component travels farthest?

options.why: Polar components stay with the polar paper.
Correct. It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.

questions.explanation: It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of chlorine shows two peaks: mass 35 with relative abundance 31% and mass 37 with 69%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 2 × 10⁻¹². At equilibrium:

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 541 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 66 kJ/mol, the transition state at 192 kJ/mol and the products at 105 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.
Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 126, ΔH = 39, reverse Ea = 87 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.8 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A 42.2 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 15.3 mL of 0.159 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = -66 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 291 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 441 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 7.9. In a solution at pH 6.7, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: 60 mL of 1.6 M solution is diluted to 212 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.17 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 7.21) and 0.44 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: Which is the strongest acid?

options.why: Correct. More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.stem: Which substance has the highest boiling point?

options.why: Correct. Water forms extensive hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 80 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 59 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -418 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -78 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.05 M solution of benzoic acid (Ka = 6.3 \times 10^{-5})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A compound (tetraphosphorus decoxide) is 43.6% P, 56.4% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to P2O5; the molecular formula is P4O10.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{AgCl}$$ is 1.8 \times 10^{-10}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

options.why: This salt gives two ions: Ksp = s².

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.39 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.2) and 0.22 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.03 mol of NaOH is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.6 mol N₂, 0.9 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.3 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.
Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 0.46 V.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$$, 63 g of $$\ce{Na}$$ reacts with 50 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NaCl}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.1 M and [I₂] = 1 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.12 M. What is K?
The first four ionization energies of an element are 885, 4425, 7700, 14245 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Correct. The large jump comes after removing 1 electron, so it has 1 valence electron.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: 11 mL of 0.2 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.18 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 4.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×4, so order 2 in B.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.042 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 53 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 7.3 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 1620 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 3 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -1.21; K = 0.298. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 3 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 5. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{5}$$, which has 9 electrons.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.72 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Mg.
Explain why the 1s peak of Mg has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Na.

rubric.criterion: Mg has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Mg has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Na: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
